title: The clock that has not started
divergence_note: This film stays outdoors in humid Houston daylight and turns one hospital exit into a split-track race. The picture travels horizontally with two date markers, then reveals that only the human route is physically wired into the work. A departing car, sunlit hospital skyline, curb, prairie grasses and moving exit gate replace the prior film's overhead municipal paper, radial civic diagram, suspended moratorium bar and dark chamber furniture.

fingerprint.palette: Houston concrete, hospital white, coastal-prairie green, bayou blue and sunlit discharge yellow
fingerprint.metaphor: two discharge-date clocks compared under different workflow conditions, then routed toward one prospective outcome test

fauna_scope.reason: The verified subject is a hospital workflow comparison; wildlife would turn a precise Harris County care-system story into decorative Gulf Coast scenery.

throughline.subject: two discharge-date markers moving toward the same sunlit hospital exit
throughline.opening_state: the case-manager and artificial-intelligence markers begin together on parallel tracks
throughline.closing_state: the two differently conditioned estimates return to a prospective outcome-test gate without a preselected winner

cinematic_contract.button: That is the next clock to start.

retime_evidence._why: A cut is placed at the start of the line its scene carries. That word's time is measured when the reader paused before it and modelled by syllable weight when they did not, so this counts both rather than claiming all are measured.

captions.text: At Houston Methodist, two estimates tried to name the same thing:
At admission, they were close on error.
Case managers still named the exact day more often.
At the later checkpoints, the case managers pulled ahead on error.
In the analysis labeled 24 hours, 79.5 percent of their estimates landed within one day.
That is when the authors say accurate dates are most actionable for bed management.
But they also name a problem with the comparison.
Case manager estimates were visible to care teams and may have become partly self-fulfilling.
The AI estimates were accessible in the record, but not enabled automatically.
So the study measured accuracy inside two different workflow conditions.
It did not measure downstream decisions or patient outcomes.
The paper calls for prospective, outcome-based testing before judging whether the extra complexity is worth it.
That is the next clock to start.
